🏢 AI-Powered Enterprise Knowledge Assistant — Capstone (Beginner Edition)¶

Module 14 capstone: an end-to-end, production-style GenAI application, built step by step in one notebook.

The fictional company Acme Retail has its knowledge scattered across PDFs, Markdown SOPs, incident reports, FAQ JSON files, SQL tables and a "who-owns-which-system" graph. Employees waste time searching for answers and depend on a few experts. In this notebook we build an assistant that fixes this:

# Capability Simple explanation Tools we use
1 Hybrid RAG Find relevant text by meaning (vector search) and by relationships (graph), then sort the best results to the top (re-ranking) ChromaDB, Neo4j, an LLM re-ranker
2 Agent with tools The LLM decides which tool to use: SQL, Python, web search, or the ticketing system LangGraph, PostgreSQL, Tavily, MCP
3 Guardrails Safety checks before and after the LLM regex + LLM checks, OpenAI moderation
4 Production layer A real HTTP API with sessions, tracing, caching and cost-aware model choice FastAPI, MongoDB, Langfuse, semantic cache
5 Evaluation Prove that it works: tests, retrieval metrics, safety and performance numbers Promptfoo, RAGAS, safety scorecard, load test

💡 How to read this notebook: every code cell has a markdown cell before it that explains what we do, why, and shows a small example. The code comments explain the individual lines. Run the cells from top to bottom (Run All). A full run takes roughly 20–30 minutes because it really calls the LLMs, databases and test tools.

🗺️ Architecture at a glance¶

Every user question travels through the same pipeline (each box is a function/node we build in this notebook):

 User question
     │
     ▼
 FastAPI  POST /chat  {message, session_id}  ─────────────► Langfuse  (traces · latency · tokens · cost · errors)
     │
     ▼
 [1] Input guardrails   validation · prompt-injection check · moderation · PII masking ──(blocked)──► refusal
     │
     ▼
 [2] Semantic cache     "was this exact question answered before?" ─────────────(hit)──► cached answer
     │
     ▼
 [3] Query router       rewrite follow-ups · retrieval needed? · simple → gpt-4o-mini / complex → gpt-4o
     │
     ▼
 [4] Hybrid retrieval   ChromaDB vector search + Neo4j graph traversal → merge → LLM re-ranker → context
     │
     ▼
 [5] LangGraph agent  ⇄  tools: query_database (PostgreSQL) · run_python · web_search (Tavily) · tickets (MCP server)
     │
     ▼
 [6] Output guardrails  secret/canary filter · moderation · PII masking · hallucination check
     │
     ▼
 JSON response: answer + sources + route + guardrails + token usage + latency + trace_id
 (the conversation is saved per session_id in MongoDB, so follow-up questions work)

0️⃣ Task 0 — Project setup¶

0.1 Create the virtual environment with uv (run once, in a terminal)¶

What is uv? uv is a very fast Python package manager. It creates a virtual environment (.venv folder): a private copy of Python with exactly the libraries this project needs, so it cannot break other projects on your computer.

The project folder already contains pyproject.toml (the list of dependencies) and uv.lock (the exact versions that were tested). Recreating the environment is therefore a single command:

pip install uv                          # 1) install uv once per machine (or: winget install astral-sh.uv)
cd langgraph-crash-course\14_capstone   # 2) go to this project folder
uv sync                                 # 3) creates .venv with Python 3.12 and installs the locked versions

This is how the project was created originally (you do not need to run it again):

uv init --bare --python 3.12
uv add langgraph langchain-openai langchain-text-splitters langchain-mcp-adapters mcp chromadb neo4j `
       "pymongo<4.18" "langgraph-checkpoint-mongodb==0.5.0" "psycopg[binary]" sqlalchemy fastapi uvicorn httpx `
       langfuse ragas "langchain-community<0.4.2" pypdf fpdf2 pandas tabulate python-dotenv truststore ipykernel nbconvert

Why the version pins? 📌 pymongo<4.18 + langgraph-checkpoint-mongodb==0.5.0 still talk to the local MongoDB 4.2 server, and langchain-community<0.4.2 is required by ragas 0.4.3. psycopg is the PostgreSQL driver and sqlalchemy lets pandas write DataFrames into PostgreSQL tables.

Finally, in VS Code choose the kernel .venv (Python 3.12) in the top-right corner of the notebook. The next cell checks that the notebook really runs inside this environment.

0.2 Configure .env (secrets) and load it¶

API keys and passwords must never be written into code. We keep them in a file called .env next to this notebook (it is listed in .gitignore, so it is never committed). A template without secrets is in .env.example:

OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...                         # LLMs + embeddings
TAVILY_API_KEY=tvly-...                       # web search tool
LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY=pk-lf-...                 # observability
LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY=sk-lf-...
LANGFUSE_BASE_URL=https://us.cloud.langfuse.com
NEO4J_URI=bolt://localhost:7687               # graph database
NEO4J_USER=neo4j
NEO4J_PASSWORD=...
NEO4J_DATABASE=capstone
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017/        # session memory
MONGODB_DB=capstone_sessions
POSTGRES_HOST=localhost                       # structured data (SQL tool)
POSTGRES_PORT=5432
POSTGRES_USER=postgres                        # admin user: creates the database and loads the tables
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=...
POSTGRES_DB=capstone_kb
POSTGRES_READONLY_USER=kb_reader              # read-only user for the agent's SQL tool (Task 5)
POSTGRES_READONLY_PASSWORD=...

load_dotenv() copies these values into os.environ. We then check that every required variable exists — we print only set / MISSING, never the secret values themselves.

We also call truststore.inject_into_ssl(): on company laptops HTTPS traffic often goes through a corporate proxy whose certificate is only in the Windows certificate store. truststore tells Python to trust that store, so calls to OpenAI, Tavily and Langfuse do not fail with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED.

In [2]:

0.3 Project folders and global settings¶

A clean folder structure makes the project easy to understand:

14_capstone/
├── data/                  ← INPUT data (we generate it in Part A)
│   ├── unstructured/      ← PDFs, Markdown and text files
│   ├── semi_structured/   ← JSON / JSON-lines files
│   ├── structured/        ← CSV tables
│   └── graph/             ← entity and relationship CSVs for Neo4j
├── storage/               ← everything the pipeline PRODUCES on disk (processed docs, Chroma index, audit log)

We also define the models in one place. Example of model routing (explained later): an easy question like "Who owns the Auth Service?" goes to the cheap gpt-4o-mini, a multi-step question goes to the stronger gpt-4o.

0.4 Smoke test — can we reach every service?¶

Before building anything we check each external service once, so a wrong password shows up now and not in the middle of the notebook:

Service Used for Check
OpenAI LLM answers, embeddings ask the model to reply "ready"
Neo4j knowledge graph verify_connectivity() + a tiny query in our database
PostgreSQL structured company data (the agent's SQL tool) read the server version + create our database capstone_kb
MongoDB session memory (chat history) read the server version
Langfuse tracing call the public health endpoint

PostgreSQL in one sentence: one PostgreSQL server (here localhost:5432) can host many databases. We connect to the always-existing maintenance database postgres, look into the catalog table pg_database, and create our own database capstone_kb only if it is missing — so running the notebook twice is safe. Two details:

  • CREATE DATABASE is not allowed inside a transaction, therefore we connect with autocommit=True.
  • Names (database/table names) are inserted with pgsql.Identifier(...), which quotes them safely. Values are passed as parameters (%s). Never build SQL with f-strings from untrusted text — that is how SQL injection happens.

neo4j_driver, mongo_client and the Postgres settings PG_SETTINGS are reused by the rest of the notebook.

In [4]:
import httpx                                 # modern HTTP client
import psycopg                               # PostgreSQL driver (version 3)
from psycopg import sql as pgsql             # helpers to build SQL with safely quoted names
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI      # LangChain wrapper around the OpenAI chat API
from neo4j import GraphDatabase              # official Neo4j driver
from pymongo import MongoClient              # official MongoDB driver

# 1) OpenAI
llm_check = ChatOpenAI(model=SIMPLE_MODEL, temperature=0, timeout=60, max_retries=1)
print("OpenAI   :", llm_check.invoke("Reply with exactly one word: ready").content)

# 2) Neo4j
neo4j_driver = GraphDatabase.driver(os.environ["NEO4J_URI"],
                                    auth=(os.environ["NEO4J_USER"], os.environ["NEO4J_PASSWORD"]),
                                    connection_timeout=15)
neo4j_driver.verify_connectivity()
records, _, _ = neo4j_driver.execute_query("RETURN 1 AS ok", database_=NEO4J_DATABASE)
print("Neo4j    : connected, database", repr(NEO4J_DATABASE), "->", records[0]["ok"])

# 3) PostgreSQL — connection settings of the ADMIN user (it creates the database and, in Task 1, the tables)
PG_SETTINGS = {
    "host": os.environ["POSTGRES_HOST"],
    "port": int(os.environ["POSTGRES_PORT"]),
    "user": os.environ["POSTGRES_USER"],
    "password": os.environ["POSTGRES_PASSWORD"],
}
with psycopg.connect(**PG_SETTINGS, dbname="postgres", autocommit=True, connect_timeout=10) as admin_connection:
    server_version = admin_connection.execute("SHOW server_version").fetchone()[0]
    # %s is a PARAMETER placeholder: psycopg sends the value separately from the SQL text (no SQL injection)
    already_exists = admin_connection.execute(
        "SELECT 1 FROM pg_database WHERE datname = %s", (POSTGRES_DB,)).fetchone() is not None
    if not already_exists:
        admin_connection.execute(pgsql.SQL("CREATE DATABASE {}").format(pgsql.Identifier(POSTGRES_DB)))
print("Postgres : server version", server_version, "| database", repr(POSTGRES_DB),
      "already exists" if already_exists else "created")

# 4) MongoDB
mongo_client = MongoClient(os.environ["MONGODB_URI"], serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000)
print("MongoDB  : server version", mongo_client.server_info()["version"])

# 5) Langfuse (public health endpoint, no key needed)
health = httpx.get(f"{os.environ['LANGFUSE_BASE_URL'].rstrip('/')}/api/public/health", timeout=30)
print("Langfuse :", health.status_code, health.json())

Neo4j    : connected, database 'capstone' -> 1

Postgres : server version 14.24 | database 'capstone_kb' already exists
MongoDB  : server version 4.2.8

🅰️ Part A — Create the synthetic enterprise dataset¶

The spec allows dummy data, so we create a small but diverse dataset for the fictional company Acme Retail. It is tiny on purpose (easy to read in a few minutes), yet it covers every data shape and every question type:

Data shape Meaning Example Our files
Unstructured free text, no fixed fields "Refunds above 500 USD require approval from the Support Manager." 3 PDFs (policies, manual), 2 SOPs (.md), 2 incident reports (.md, .txt)
Semi-structured has keys/values but flexible and nested {"level": "ERROR", "context": {"host": "pg-01"}} faq.json, support_tickets.json, service_logs.jsonl
Structured rows and columns with a fixed schema T1007,U003,P003,1,329.00,credit_card,failed,2024-03-12 products.csv, users.csv, transactions.csv, table_metadata.csv
Graph entities + relationships (Alice Chen)-[:OWNS]->(Checkout Service) entities.csv, relationships.csv

The four business domains from the spec are covered: Engineering (deployment SOP, systems), Operations (on-call manual, incidents, logs), Compliance (privacy policy) and Customer Support (refund policy, password SOP, FAQ, tickets).

🔗 The sources are deliberately connected, so the assistant can combine them. Example: the payment outage incident INC-2024-017 happened on 2024-03-12 → on that date the transactions table has two failed payments, the service_logs show TLS ERRORs and support ticket TCK-1001 was opened.

A.1 Policy and manual PDFs (unstructured)¶

Real companies keep policies as PDFs, so we generate three small PDFs with the fpdf2 library:

  • data_privacy_policy.pdf (Compliance) — retention periods, deletion requests, encryption, breach reporting
  • refund_policy.pdf (Customer Support) — refund window, processing time, approvals, exceptions
  • oncall_incident_manual.pdf (Operations) — severity levels, response times, escalation, postmortems

Every document starts with the same header fields (Document ID, Domain, Owner, Effective date). In Task 1 we will extract these fields automatically as metadata.

ℹ️ The built-in PDF font only supports basic Latin characters, so the texts use plain ASCII (- instead of –).

In [5]:
from fpdf import FPDF   # fpdf2: a small library to create PDF files


def write_pdf(path, title, header_lines, sections):
    """Create a simple PDF: a title, some header lines and numbered sections (heading + paragraph)."""
    pdf = FPDF()
    pdf.set_auto_page_break(auto=True, margin=15)     # start a new page automatically when a page is full
    pdf.add_page()
    pdf.set_font("Helvetica", "B", 16)                 # B = bold, size 16 for the title
    pdf.multi_cell(0, 10, title, new_x="LMARGIN", new_y="NEXT")
    pdf.set_font("Helvetica", "", 10)
    for line in header_lines:                          # one short metadata line per row
        pdf.multi_cell(0, 6, line, new_x="LMARGIN", new_y="NEXT")
    pdf.ln(4)                                          # a little vertical space
    for heading, paragraph in sections:
        pdf.set_font("Helvetica", "B", 12)
        pdf.multi_cell(0, 8, heading, new_x="LMARGIN", new_y="NEXT")
        pdf.set_font("Helvetica", "", 11)
        pdf.multi_cell(0, 6, paragraph, new_x="LMARGIN", new_y="NEXT")   # multi_cell wraps long text
        pdf.ln(2)
    pdf.output(str(path))

A.2 SOPs and incident reports (Markdown and plain text)¶

Engineers usually write procedures (SOPs) and incident reports in Markdown or plain text. We create four files:

File Domain Typical question it answers
sop_checkout_deployment.md Engineering "What is the rollback command for checkout?"
sop_password_reset.md Customer Support "How long is a password reset link valid?"
incident_INC-2024-017_payment_outage.md Operations "What caused the payment outage?"
incident_INC-2024-021_redis_cache.txt Operations "How was the Redis incident fixed?"

Notice the Markdown formatting (# headings, **bold**, lists). Task 1 cleans this formatting away.

In [6]:
# Each document is a normal multi-line Python string that we write to a file.
documents_to_write = {
"sop_checkout_deployment.md": """# SOP-ENG-004: Deploying the Checkout Service

**Domain:** Engineering
**Owner:** Alice Chen (Checkout Team Lead)
**Last updated:** 2024-04-02

## Before you deploy
1. Make sure all CI tests are green on the main branch.
2. Deployments are not allowed on Fridays after 14:00 UTC.
3. Announce the deployment in the #deployments Slack channel.

## Canary release
1. Release the new version to 10% of traffic (the canary) for 30 minutes.
2. Watch the dashboards: the error rate must stay below 1% and the p95 latency below 800 ms.
3. If both checks pass, roll out to 100% of traffic.

## Rollback
- Roll back immediately if the error rate goes above 2%.
- Rollback command: `deployctl rollback checkout --to previous`
- After a rollback, open a SEV2 incident and inform the Checkout team lead (Alice Chen).

## Dependencies to verify
The Checkout Service depends on the Payment Gateway, the Inventory Service, the Auth Service and the Redis Cache.
Check that all four are healthy before you start.
""",

"sop_password_reset.md": """# SOP-SUP-002: Customer Password Reset

**Domain:** Customer Support
**Owner:** Sofia Rossi (Support Manager)
**Last updated:** 2024-03-18

## Steps
1. Verify the identity of the customer: ask for the email address of the account and the last order ID.
2. Never ask the customer for their password, full card number or one-time codes.
3. Trigger the reset in the admin console: Users > Select user > Send reset link.
4. The reset link is valid for 1 hour.

## Locked accounts
- Accounts are locked after 5 failed login attempts.
- Locked accounts unlock automatically after 30 minutes, or support can unlock them after identity verification.

## Escalation
If the reset email does not arrive within 10 minutes, escalate to the Auth Service on-call engineer
(owner: Tom Becker). The Auth Service sends reset emails through the Notification Service.
""",

"incident_INC-2024-017_payment_outage.md": """# Incident Report INC-2024-017: Payment Gateway Outage

- **Domain:** Operations
- **Owner:** Ravi Kumar (Payment Gateway owner, incident commander)
- **Date:** 2024-03-12
- **Duration:** 45 minutes (09:05-09:50 UTC)
- **Severity:** SEV1
- **Affected systems:** Payment Gateway, Checkout Service

## Summary
Customers could not complete card payments for 45 minutes. About 1,200 checkouts failed.
The estimated revenue impact was 85,000 USD.

## Root cause
The TLS certificate of the Payment Gateway expired. Automatic certificate renewal had been disabled
during a server migration in February and was never turned back on.

## Resolution
The certificate was renewed manually at 09:45 UTC and payments recovered by 09:50 UTC.

## Action items
1. Re-enable automatic certificate renewal (owner: Ravi Kumar) - done.
2. Add an alert 30 days before any certificate expires (owner: Ben Ortiz).
3. Add certificate checks to the server migration checklist.
""",

"incident_INC-2024-021_redis_cache.txt": """INCIDENT REPORT INC-2024-021 - Redis Cache Memory Exhaustion
Domain: Operations
Owner: Ben Ortiz (SRE Lead, incident commander)
Date: 2024-05-02
Duration: 80 minutes (14:10-15:30 UTC)
Severity: SEV2
Affected systems: Redis Cache, Checkout Service, Auth Service

SUMMARY
The Redis Cache ran out of memory. The p95 latency of the checkout rose from 600 ms to 4 seconds,
and some users were logged out because the Auth Service stores sessions in Redis.

ROOT CAUSE
A code change stored session keys without an expiry time (TTL), so memory filled up over three days.

RESOLUTION
A 24 hour TTL was added to all session keys and Redis memory was increased from 8 GB to 16 GB.

ACTION ITEMS
- Add an alert when Redis memory usage goes above 80% (owner: Ben Ortiz).
- Add a code review checklist item: every cache key must have a TTL (owner: Alice Chen).
""",
}

for file_name, content in documents_to_write.items():
    (UNSTRUCTURED_DIR / file_name).write_text(content, encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"created {file_name:42} {len(content):>5} characters")

A.3 Semi-structured data: FAQ, support tickets and service logs¶

Semi-structured data has keys, but records can differ and fields can be nested (a dict inside a dict or a list):

  • faq.json — 8 knowledge-base articles (question, answer, category, tags list). Each FAQ becomes a searchable document.
  • support_tickets.json — 6 tickets with a nested customer object and optional comments / resolution. These are served by the MCP ticketing server (Section 5), like a real external ticketing API.
  • service_logs.jsonl — JSON Lines: one JSON object per line (very common for logs), with a nested context. In Task 1 we flatten them into a SQL table, e.g. context.host → column context_host.

Example of one log line:

{"timestamp": "2024-03-12T09:05:10Z", "level": "ERROR", "service": "Payment Gateway",
 "message": "TLS handshake failed: certificate has expired", "context": {"host": "pg-01", "latency_ms": 30}}

A.4 Structured data: products, users, transactions and a metadata table¶

Structured data is the easiest to query precisely with SQL. We write the CSV files as plain text, so you can see exactly what is inside. The values were chosen so that typical business questions have clear answers (we use them later as test expectations):

Question Answer from the data
How many gold tier users? 3 (U001, U004, U007)
Total revenue of completed transactions? 1,700.95 USD (11 completed transactions)
Top category by completed revenue? Electronics (1,313.95 USD)
Failed transactions? T1007, T1008 — both on 2024-03-12 (the payment outage day)
Out-of-stock products? Standing Desk (P005)
Top customer by completed spend? Arjun Patel (U007, 553.99 USD)

table_metadata.csv is a metadata table (a data dictionary): it describes every column, including the allowed values. The agent can read it to understand the database. The users table contains PII (emails, phone numbers) on purpose, so we can show that the guardrails mask it.

A.5 Graph data: entities and relationships¶

Some questions are about relationships, not text. Example: "If the Message Queue goes down, which systems are affected?" The answer is a chain: Notification Service depends on the Message Queue → Payment Gateway depends on the Notification Service → Checkout Service depends on the Payment Gateway. Vector search cannot follow such chains; a graph can (this is called multi-hop reasoning).

  • entities.csv — 18 entities: 6 people, 5 systems, 3 components, 2 incidents, 2 policies. aliases lists other names users might type (e.g. redis for Redis Cache), separated by |.
  • relationships.csv — the three relationship types from the spec: OWNS (person → system/policy), DEPENDS_ON (system → system/component), RELATED_TO (incident/policy ↔ system).
Alice Chen ──OWNS──► Checkout Service ──DEPENDS_ON──► Payment Gateway ──DEPENDS_ON──► Notification Service ──DEPENDS_ON──► Message Queue
In [9]:

A.6 Dataset inventory¶

A quick overview of everything we just created — 16 small files in 4 folders. This is the complete input of the system. Everything else (indexes, databases, graph) is derived from these files by the pipeline, so you can delete storage/ at any time and simply re-run the notebook.

In [10]:
inventory = []
for path in sorted(DATA_DIR.rglob("*")):           # rglob("*") = all files in all sub-folders
    if path.is_file():
        inventory.append({"folder": path.parent.name, "file": path.name, "kb": round(path.stat().st_size / 1024, 1)})

inventory_df = pd.DataFrame(inventory)

1️⃣ Task 1 — Data ingestion and preprocessing¶

Goal: turn the messy input files into one clean, uniform list of documents with metadata.

PDF / Markdown / TXT / FAQ-JSON ──load──► raw text ──clean──► clean text ──extract──► metadata ──store──► documents.jsonl + PostgreSQL

Every processed document becomes one Python dictionary, for example:

{"doc_id": "POL-002", "title": "Refund Policy", "doc_type": "policy", "domain": "Customer Support",
 "owner": "Sofia Rossi", "date": "2024-02-01", "source": "refund_policy.pdf", "file_type": "pdf",
 "pages": 1, "char_count": 1290, "text": "Refund Policy\nDocument ID: POL-002\n..."}

Why metadata? It lets us filter (search only Compliance documents), cite ("source: refund_policy.pdf") and rank (the re-ranker sees the document title next to every chunk).

1.1 Loading and cleaning functions¶

Function What it does Example
load_pdf reads the text of every page with pypdf refund_policy.pdf → text + number of pages
load_text_file reads Markdown / .txt files sop_password_reset.md → text
clean_text Unicode normalisation, unified line endings, removes Markdown **bold** markers, collapses spaces, max. one empty line "**Owner:** Alice" → "Owner: Alice"
fix_pdf_line_breaks a PDF stores every printed line separately, so sentences are cut in the middle; we glue them together again "retained for⏎2 years" → "retained for 2 years"
In [11]:
import unicodedata              # Unicode normalisation (part of the standard library)
from pypdf import PdfReader     # reads the text out of PDF files


def load_pdf(path):
    """Return (text, number_of_pages) for a PDF file."""
    reader = PdfReader(str(path))
    page_texts = [page.extract_text() or "" for page in reader.pages]   # "or ''" protects against empty pages
    return "\n".join(page_texts), len(reader.pages)


def load_text_file(path):
    """Markdown and .txt files are plain text, so we simply read them (we count them as 1 page)."""
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"), 1


def clean_text(text):
    """Normalise text so that every document looks the same, whatever its original format was."""
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)              # e.g. ligature 'ﬁ' -> 'fi', non-breaking space -> space
    text = text.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n")   # Windows / old Mac line endings -> '\n'
    text = text.replace("**", "")                           # Markdown bold markers: '**Owner:**' -> 'Owner:'
    text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+", " ", text)                     # several spaces or tabs -> one space
    text = re.sub(r" *\n *", "\n", text)                    # no spaces at the start or end of a line
    text = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", text)                  # at most ONE empty line between paragraphs
    return text.strip()                                     # no whitespace at the very start / end


def fix_pdf_line_breaks(text):
    """Glue sentences together that the PDF split over two lines.
    Rule: if a line ends with a lowercase letter or a comma AND the next line starts with a lowercase
    letter or a digit, the sentence simply continues -> replace the line break with a space.
    Headings such as '2. Data retention' start with a digit but follow a '.', so they stay on their own line."""
    return re.sub(r"(?<=[a-z,])\n(?=[a-z0-9])", " ", text)


# Small demonstration with a deliberately messy string
messy = "**Owner:**   Alice   Chen\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nRefunds are  issued within\n5-7 business days."
print("BEFORE:", repr(messy))
print("AFTER :", repr(fix_pdf_line_breaks(clean_text(messy))))

BEFORE: '**Owner:**   Alice   Chen\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nRefunds are  issued within\n5-7 business days.'
AFTER : 'Owner: Alice Chen\n\nRefunds are issued within 5-7 business days.'

1.2 Extract metadata with regular expressions¶

All our documents follow the same header convention, so simple regular expressions (text patterns) can find the metadata fields automatically:

Field Pattern (simplified) Example input → value
doc_id POL-123, MAN-123, SOP-ABC-123, INC-2024-123 Document ID: POL-001 → POL-001
doc_type first part of the id SOP-ENG-004 → SOP → sop
title the first line (without Markdown #) # SOP-ENG-004: Deploying ... → SOP-ENG-004: Deploying ...
domain letters after Domain: Domain: Compliance → Compliance
owner letters after Owner: (stops at () Owner: Priya Sharma (Data Protection Officer) → Priya Sharma
date first YYYY-MM-DD Effective date: 2024-01-15 → 2024-01-15

If a field is missing, find_first raises a clear error instead of silently storing an empty value.

In [12]:
DOC_ID_PATTERN = r"\b(POL-\d{3}|MAN-\d{3}|SOP-[A-Z]{3}-\d{3}|INC-\d{4}-\d{3})\b"   # e.g. POL-001, SOP-ENG-004, INC-2024-017
DOC_TYPES = {"POL": "policy", "MAN": "manual", "SOP": "sop", "INC": "incident_report"}


def find_first(pattern, text):
    """Return the first captured group of a regex pattern, or raise a clear error if it is missing."""
    match = re.search(pattern, text)
    if match is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Pattern {pattern!r} not found - every document needs this field")
    return match.group(1).strip()


def extract_metadata(text, path, pages):
    """Build the metadata dictionary of one document from its cleaned text and file path."""
    doc_id = find_first(DOC_ID_PATTERN, text)
    return {
        "doc_id": doc_id,
        "title": text.split("\n", 1)[0].lstrip("#").strip(),     # first line, without the Markdown '#'
        "doc_type": DOC_TYPES[doc_id.split("-")[0]],             # 'SOP-ENG-004' -> 'SOP' -> 'sop'
        "domain": find_first(r"Domain:\s*([A-Za-z ]+)", text),   # letters/spaces after 'Domain:'
        "owner": find_first(r"Owner:\s*([A-Za-z ]+)", text),     # stops at '(' -> only the person's name
        "date": find_first(r"(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})", text),        # first date in the document
        "source": path.name,                                     # file name, used for citations
        "file_type": path.suffix.lstrip("."),                    # '.pdf' -> 'pdf'
        "pages": pages,
        "char_count": len(text),
    }


# Try it on one Markdown file
example_path = UNSTRUCTURED_DIR / "sop_checkout_deployment.md"
example_text = clean_text(load_text_file(example_path)[0])
extract_metadata(example_text, example_path, pages=1)

1.3 Process all documents and store them¶

  • Unstructured files (PDF, .md, .txt): load → clean → (PDF only: fix line breaks) → extract metadata.
  • FAQ (semi-structured JSON): every question/answer pair becomes its own small document. Here we do not need regular expressions — the JSON already has fields (category, owner, last_reviewed) that we map to our metadata.
  • The result is stored as JSON Lines in storage/processed/documents.jsonl (one document per line), so later steps (or another program) can reload the clean corpus without repeating the work.

Expected result: 7 files + 8 FAQ articles = 15 documents across the 4 business domains.

In [13]:
documents = []

# 1) Unstructured files: PDFs, Markdown and plain text
for path in sorted(UNSTRUCTURED_DIR.iterdir()):
    if path.suffix == ".pdf":
        raw_text, pages = load_pdf(path)
        text = fix_pdf_line_breaks(clean_text(raw_text))
    else:                                              # .md and .txt files
        raw_text, pages = load_text_file(path)
        text = clean_text(raw_text)
    document = extract_metadata(text, path, pages)
    document["text"] = text
    documents.append(document)

# 2) Semi-structured FAQ: every question/answer pair becomes one small document
faq_items = json.loads((SEMI_STRUCTURED_DIR / "faq.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
for item in faq_items:
    text = clean_text(f"Question: {item['question']}\nAnswer: {item['answer']}")
    documents.append({
        "doc_id": item["id"], "title": item["question"], "doc_type": "faq", "domain": item["category"],
        "owner": item["owner"], "date": item["last_reviewed"], "source": "faq.json", "file_type": "json",
        "pages": 1, "char_count": len(text), "text": text,
    })

# 3) Store the processed corpus as JSON Lines (one JSON document per line)
processed_file = PROCESSED_DIR / "documents.jsonl"
with open(processed_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for document in documents:
        f.write(json.dumps(document, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

documents_df = pd.DataFrame(documents)
print(f"Processed {len(documents)} documents -> {processed_file.relative_to(BASE_DIR)}")
print(documents_df["domain"].value_counts().to_string())       # documents per business domain
documents_df.drop(columns=["text"])                             # show the metadata table (without the long text)

1.4 Load structured and semi-structured data into PostgreSQL¶

The agent will answer numeric questions ("total revenue?", "how many errors on 2024-03-12?") with SQL, so we load the tabular data into our PostgreSQL database capstone_kb (created in step 0.4):

Table Comes from Note
products, users, transactions CSV files structured data
table_metadata CSV file the data dictionary — describes every column (the agent reads it)
service_logs service_logs.jsonl semi-structured → flattened: nested context.host becomes column context_host
document_metadata the processed documents a metadata table of the document corpus

pd.json_normalize does the flattening. Example: {"level": "ERROR", "context": {"host": "pg-01"}} → columns level = ERROR, context.host = pg-01 → we rename context.host to context_host (dots are awkward in SQL).

Data types matter. A CSV file contains only text, so we tell PostgreSQL what each column really is:

Columns Conversion in pandas PostgreSQL type Why
signup_date, transaction_date, date pd.to_datetime(...).dt.date date date comparisons work: WHERE transaction_date >= '2024-03-01'
timestamp (logs) pd.to_datetime(..., utc=True) timestamp with time zone e.g. WHERE timestamp::date = '2024-03-12'
price_usd, amount_usd dtype={...: Numeric(10, 2)} numeric(10,2) exact money values (no floating-point rounding), ROUND(SUM(amount_usd), 2) works
all other columns automatic text, bigint

pandas.to_sql needs a SQLAlchemy engine — a small "connection factory". Its URL postgresql+psycopg://postgres:***@localhost:5432/capstone_kb means: database type PostgreSQL, driver psycopg, user, password, server, port and database name. if_exists="replace" drops and recreates each table, so the cell can be re-run safely. Finally we ask PostgreSQL's own catalog (information_schema.columns) which types it created.

In [15]:
from sqlalchemy import Numeric, create_engine      # SQLAlchemy: lets pandas talk to PostgreSQL
from sqlalchemy.engine import URL

tables = {
    "products": pd.read_csv(STRUCTURED_DIR / "products.csv"),
    "users": pd.read_csv(STRUCTURED_DIR / "users.csv"),
    "transactions": pd.read_csv(STRUCTURED_DIR / "transactions.csv"),
    "table_metadata": pd.read_csv(STRUCTURED_DIR / "table_metadata.csv"),
}

# Semi-structured JSON Lines -> flat table
log_lines = (SEMI_STRUCTURED_DIR / "service_logs.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
log_records = [json.loads(line) for line in log_lines if line.strip()]      # one dict per non-empty line
logs_df = pd.json_normalize(log_records)                                    # nested dicts -> 'context.host' columns
logs_df.columns = [column.replace(".", "_") for column in logs_df.columns]  # 'context.host' -> 'context_host'
tables["service_logs"] = logs_df

# Metadata table of the processed documents (e.g. "which documents does Compliance own?")
tables["document_metadata"] = documents_df[["doc_id", "title", "doc_type", "domain", "owner", "date", "source"]].copy()

# Give date/time columns their real type (pandas -> PostgreSQL 'date' / 'timestamp with time zone')
for table_df in tables.values():
    for column in table_df.columns:
        if column.endswith("date"):                                    # signup_date, transaction_date, date
            table_df[column] = pd.to_datetime(table_df[column]).dt.date
        elif column == "timestamp":                                    # log time, always UTC
            table_df[column] = pd.to_datetime(table_df[column], utc=True)
MONEY_COLUMNS = {"price_usd": Numeric(10, 2), "amount_usd": Numeric(10, 2)}    # exact decimals with 2 digits

pg_engine = create_engine(
    URL.create("postgresql+psycopg",                     # database type + driver
               username=PG_SETTINGS["user"], password=PG_SETTINGS["password"],
               host=PG_SETTINGS["host"], port=PG_SETTINGS["port"], database=POSTGRES_DB),
    connect_args={"options": "-c TimeZone=UTC"},          # show all times in UTC
)

for table_name, table_df in tables.items():
    money_types = {column: MONEY_COLUMNS[column] for column in table_df.columns if column in MONEY_COLUMNS}
    table_df.to_sql(table_name, pg_engine, if_exists="replace", index=False, dtype=money_types)   # replace -> re-runnable
    print(f"{table_name:18} {len(table_df):>3} rows | columns: {', '.join(table_df.columns)}")

# Which data types did PostgreSQL create? (information_schema = the database's own description of itself)
type_query = ("SELECT column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns "
              "WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name = 'transactions' ORDER BY ordinal_position")
print("\nColumn types of 'transactions':")
print(pd.read_sql_query(type_query, pg_engine).to_string(index=False))

# A first SQL query to prove it works: ERROR log lines per service
test_query = ("SELECT service, COUNT(*) AS errors FROM service_logs "
              "WHERE level = 'ERROR' GROUP BY service ORDER BY errors DESC, service")
print("\n" + test_query)
print(pd.read_sql_query(test_query, pg_engine).to_string(index=False))

2️⃣ Task 2 — Vector indexing (ChromaDB)¶

Semantic search finds text by meaning, not by exact words. Example: the question "For how many years must we keep purchase records?" finds the sentence "Customer transaction records are retained for 7 years", although the words "keep" and "purchase" never appear in it. Four steps: chunk → embed → store → validate.

2.1 Chunking¶

LLMs and embeddings work best with short, focused pieces of text (chunks) instead of whole documents:

  • chunk_size=500 characters ≈ one or two paragraphs — small enough to be precise, big enough to keep a full rule.
  • chunk_overlap=80 — neighbouring chunks share ~80 characters, so a sentence cut at a border is still complete in one of them.
  • RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter tries to split at paragraph breaks first, then line breaks, then sentences, then words.
  • Every chunk gets the document title as prefix, e.g. [Refund Policy], so even a small chunk "knows" what it is about, and a stable id such as POL-002::chunk1 plus the document metadata (for filtering and citations).
In [16]:
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=80)

chunks = []
for document in documents:
    for index, piece in enumerate(splitter.split_text(document["text"])):
        metadata = {key: document[key] for key in ["doc_id", "title", "doc_type", "domain", "owner", "source"]}
        metadata["chunk_index"] = index
        chunks.append({
            "id": f"{document['doc_id']}::chunk{index}",     # unique and readable, e.g. 'POL-002::chunk1'
            "text": f"[{document['title']}]\n{piece}",        # the title prefix gives every chunk its context
            "metadata": metadata,
        })

chunk_lengths = pd.Series([len(chunk["text"]) for chunk in chunks])
print(f"{len(documents)} documents -> {len(chunks)} chunks "
      f"(characters per chunk: min {chunk_lengths.min()}, mean {chunk_lengths.mean():.0f}, max {chunk_lengths.max()})")
print("\nExample chunk", chunks[1]["id"], "with metadata", chunks[1]["metadata"])
print(chunks[1]["text"])

15 documents -> 27 chunks (characters per chunk: min 166, mean 363, max 529)

Example chunk POL-001::chunk1 with metadata {'doc_id': 'POL-001', 'title': 'Data Privacy Policy', 'doc_type': 'policy', 'domain': 'Compliance', 'owner': 'Priya Sharma', 'source': 'data_privacy_policy.pdf', 'chunk_index': 1}
[Data Privacy Policy]
years after they are closed. Application logs are retained for 90 days and must never contain full card numbers.
3. Deletion requests
Customers can request deletion of their personal data through the Privacy Portal. Deletion requests must be completed within 30 days. Transaction records are exempt until the 7 year retention period ends.
4. Security controls

2.2 Embeddings + storage in ChromaDB¶

An embedding is a list of numbers (here 1,536) that represents the meaning of a text. Texts with similar meaning get similar vectors. We use OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and store chunks + vectors + metadata in ChromaDB, a local vector database that saves its files in storage/chroma/.

  • metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"} → Chroma measures cosine distance: 0 = same meaning, larger = less similar. We report similarity = 1 - distance, which is easier to read (1.0 = identical).
  • We delete and re-create the collection on every run, so the index always matches the current documents.
In [17]:
import chromadb
from chromadb.config import Settings
from chromadb.utils.embedding_functions import OpenAIEmbeddingFunction

chroma_client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=str(CHROMA_DIR), settings=Settings(anonymized_telemetry=False))
embedding_function = OpenAIEmbeddingFunction(api_key_env_var="OPENAI_API_KEY", model_name=EMBEDDING_MODEL)

# Re-runnable: remove the old collection first (if it exists)
if "knowledge_base" in [existing.name for existing in chroma_client.list_collections()]:
    chroma_client.delete_collection("knowledge_base")

collection = chroma_client.create_collection(
    name="knowledge_base",
    embedding_function=embedding_function,    # Chroma calls OpenAI to embed our chunks AND later the queries
    metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"},        # use cosine distance
)
collection.add(                               # embeds all chunks (one API call) and stores them on disk
    ids=[chunk["id"] for chunk in chunks],
    documents=[chunk["text"] for chunk in chunks],
    metadatas=[chunk["metadata"] for chunk in chunks],
)
print("Chunks stored in ChromaDB:", collection.count())

example_vector = embedding_function(["refund window"])[0]
print(f"One embedding has {len(example_vector)} numbers. The first five: {[round(float(x), 4) for x in example_vector[:5]]}")

Chunks stored in ChromaDB: 27

One embedding has 1536 numbers. The first five: [-0.0616, 0.0543, 0.0164, 0.0154, -0.0482]

2.3 Vector search + validation¶

vector_search(query, k, domain) embeds the query and returns the k closest chunks. The optional domain argument is a metadata filter (e.g. only Compliance documents).

Validate retrieval: we ask 8 questions whose correct document we know, worded differently from the documents, and measure:

  • Hit rate @4 — in how many cases is the correct document among the top 4 results? (goal: 100 %)
  • MRR (mean reciprocal rank) — rank 1 scores 1.0, rank 2 scores 0.5, rank 3 scores 0.33 ... (goal: close to 1.0)
In [18]:
def vector_search(query, k=4, domain=None):
    """Return the k chunks whose meaning is closest to the query (optionally only from one business domain)."""
    result = collection.query(
        query_texts=[query],
        n_results=k,
        where={"domain": domain} if domain else None,      # metadata filter, e.g. {"domain": "Compliance"}
    )
    hits = []
    # Chroma returns one list per query; we sent one query, so we take element [0] of each list
    for chunk_id, text, metadata, distance in zip(result["ids"][0], result["documents"][0],
                                                  result["metadatas"][0], result["distances"][0]):
        hits.append({"id": chunk_id, "text": text, "doc_id": metadata["doc_id"], "title": metadata["title"],
                     "source": metadata["source"], "domain": metadata["domain"],
                     "similarity": round(1 - distance, 3), "retriever": "vector"})
    return hits


validation_set = [   # (question worded differently from the document, document that contains the answer)
    ("For how many years must we keep customer purchase records?", "POL-001"),
    ("How many business days until refunded money reaches the customer?", "POL-002"),
    ("How quickly must a SEV1 incident be acknowledged?", "MAN-001"),
    ("Which command undoes a bad checkout release?", "SOP-ENG-004"),
    ("For how long can a customer use a password reset link?", "SOP-SUP-002"),
    ("Why did card payments fail in March 2024?", "INC-2024-017"),
    ("What caused the Redis cache to run out of memory?", "INC-2024-021"),
    ("What does express delivery cost?", "FAQ-002"),
]

rows = []
for question, expected_doc in validation_set:
    hits = vector_search(question, k=4)
    found_docs = [hit["doc_id"] for hit in hits]
    rank = found_docs.index(expected_doc) + 1 if expected_doc in found_docs else None   # 1 = best position
    rows.append({"question": question, "expected": expected_doc, "rank": rank,
                 "top_hit": hits[0]["id"], "top_similarity": hits[0]["similarity"]})

validation_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
hit_rate = validation_df["rank"].notna().mean()
mrr = validation_df["rank"].apply(lambda r: 1 / r if pd.notna(r) else 0).mean()
print(f"Hit rate @4: {hit_rate:.0%}   |   MRR: {mrr:.2f}")
validation_df

Metadata filtering in action. The vague question "How long do we keep data?" matches retention rules from several domains. With domain="Compliance" we restrict the search to the Compliance documents only — useful when, for example, the Compliance team uses the assistant.

3️⃣ Task 3 — Knowledge graph construction (Neo4j)¶

Vector search cannot follow chains of facts. "If the Message Queue goes down, which systems are affected?" needs: Notification Service → depends on → Message Queue, Payment Gateway → depends on → Notification Service, and so on. A graph database stores exactly such facts as nodes (entities) and relationships (edges) and can follow them over several hops (multi-hop reasoning).

Cypher in 30 seconds (Neo4j's query language — patterns look like ASCII art):

Cypher Meaning
MERGE (e:Entity {name: "Alice Chen"}) create the node if it does not exist yet (no duplicates)
MATCH (p:Person)-[:OWNS]->(s) RETURN p.name, s.name find every person → OWNS → something pattern
-[:DEPENDS_ON*1..3]-> follow 1 to 3 DEPENDS_ON relationships in a row (multi-hop!)
$name a parameter — values are passed separately, never pasted into the query text (prevents injection)

3.1 Load the curated entities and relationships¶

run_cypher is a tiny helper around the driver. add_entity / add_relationship use MERGE, so running the cell twice does not create duplicates. Every node gets the general label Entity plus its type label (:Entity:System). Node types and relationship types are checked against an allow-list before they are written.

In [20]:
def run_cypher(query, **params):
    """Run a Cypher query in our Neo4j database and return the rows as a list of dicts."""
    records, _, _ = neo4j_driver.execute_query(query, params, database_=NEO4J_DATABASE)
    return [record.data() for record in records]


ENTITY_TYPES = {"Person", "System", "Component", "Incident", "Policy"}
RELATION_TYPES = {"OWNS", "DEPENDS_ON", "RELATED_TO"}


def add_entity(name, entity_type, description="", aliases=(), source="csv"):
    """Create one node, e.g. (:Entity:System {name: 'Payment Gateway', ...}), unless it already exists."""
    if entity_type not in ENTITY_TYPES:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown entity type: {entity_type}")
    # Labels cannot be $parameters in Cypher, so the label is added as text.
    # This is safe ONLY because entity_type was checked against the allow-list above.
    run_cypher("MERGE (e:Entity {name: $name}) "
               "ON CREATE SET e:" + entity_type + ", e.type = $type, e.description = $description, "
               "e.aliases = $aliases, e.source = $source",
               name=name, type=entity_type, description=description, aliases=list(aliases), source=source)


def add_relationship(source_name, relation, target_name, source="csv"):
    """Create (source)-[:RELATION]->(target) between two existing nodes, unless it already exists."""
    if relation not in RELATION_TYPES:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown relation type: {relation}")
    run_cypher("MATCH (a:Entity {name: $a}), (b:Entity {name: $b}) "
               "MERGE (a)-[r:" + relation + "]->(b) ON CREATE SET r.source = $source",
               a=source_name, b=target_name, source=source)


# Start from an empty graph, so the notebook can be re-run safely
run_cypher("MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n")                 # DETACH = delete the node AND its relationships
run_cypher("CREATE CONSTRAINT entity_name IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Entity) REQUIRE e.name IS UNIQUE")

entities_df = pd.read_csv(GRAPH_DATA_DIR / "entities.csv").fillna("")    # fillna: empty cells -> ""
relationships_df = pd.read_csv(GRAPH_DATA_DIR / "relationships.csv")

for row in entities_df.itertuples():
    aliases = [alias.strip() for alias in row.aliases.split("|") if alias.strip()]   # "auth|login" -> ["auth", "login"]
    add_entity(row.name, row.type, row.description, aliases)
for row in relationships_df.itertuples():
    add_relationship(row.source, row.relation, row.target)

print(pd.DataFrame(run_cypher("MATCH (n:Entity) RETURN n.type AS type, count(*) AS nodes ORDER BY nodes DESC")).to_string(index=False))

3.2 Extract entities and relations from the documents with an LLM¶

The CSV files contain curated knowledge, but the documents contain more facts. Example — the password SOP says "The Auth Service sends reset emails through the Notification Service": a dependency that is not in the CSV.

We ask the LLM to return the entities and relationships of each document as structured output (a Pydantic model), then validate every item before it touches the graph — an LLM can make mistakes, and wrong facts in a graph are hard to spot later:

  1. Entity resolution — names and aliases are mapped to existing nodes ("redis" → Redis Cache, "Incident INC-2024-017" → INC-2024-017).
  2. No invented entities — a new entity is accepted only if its name literally appears in the document.
  3. Schema check — e.g. OWNS must go from a Person to a System/Component/Policy.
  4. Only new knowledge — if two entities are already connected, we keep the curated relationship.

Everything the LLM adds is tagged source = "llm_extracted", so machine-made knowledge is always visible (and removable). We use the stronger gpt-4o here because extraction errors would end up permanently in the graph.

In [21]:
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from IPython.display import display


class ExtractedEntity(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(description="Name exactly as written in the document, e.g. 'Payment Gateway'")
    type: Literal["Person", "System", "Component", "Incident", "Policy"]
    description: str = Field(description="One short sentence describing the entity")


class ExtractedRelation(BaseModel):
    source: str = Field(description="Name of the source entity")
    relation: Literal["OWNS", "DEPENDS_ON", "RELATED_TO"]
    target: str = Field(description="Name of the target entity")


class GraphExtraction(BaseModel):
    entities: list[ExtractedEntity]
    relations: list[ExtractedRelation]


extractor_llm = ChatOpenAI(model=COMPLEX_MODEL, temperature=0, timeout=90, max_retries=2).with_structured_output(GraphExtraction)

EXTRACTION_PROMPT = """Extract a knowledge graph from the company document below.
Entity types: Person, System (software service), Component (database, cache, queue), Incident, Policy.
Do not extract teams, departments, Slack channels, commands, tools or the company itself.
Relationship types (the direction matters!):
- OWNS: a Person owns or leads a System, Component or Policy
- DEPENDS_ON: a System/Component needs another System/Component to work (A DEPENDS_ON B means A uses B)
- RELATED_TO: an Incident or Policy concerns a System/Component, or a Person was involved in an Incident
Only extract facts that the text states explicitly.
If an entity is one of these known entities, use exactly the known name: {known_names}

Document:
{text}"""

# For every relation: which entity types may be at the start and at the end
EDGE_SCHEMA = {
    "OWNS": ({"Person"}, {"System", "Component", "Policy"}),
    "DEPENDS_ON": ({"System", "Component"}, {"System", "Component"}),
    "RELATED_TO": (ENTITY_TYPES, ENTITY_TYPES),
}

# Lookup tables for entity resolution: every name and alias (lower case) -> official node name
name_lookup = {}
entity_type_of = {}
for row in entities_df.itertuples():
    name_lookup[row.name.lower()] = row.name
    entity_type_of[row.name] = row.type
    for alias in row.aliases.split("|"):
        if alias.strip():
            name_lookup[alias.strip().lower()] = row.name


def resolve_entity(name):
    """Map a name written by the LLM to an existing node name, or return None if the entity is unknown."""
    key = name.strip().lower()
    if key in name_lookup:                                 # exact name or alias: 'redis' -> 'Redis Cache'
        return name_lookup[key]
    contained = [known for known in entity_type_of if known.lower() in key]
    if contained:                                          # 'Incident INC-2024-017' -> 'INC-2024-017'
        return max(contained, key=len)                     # the longest (= most specific) known name
    return None


# Pairs of entities that are already connected (in either direction)
connected_pairs = set()
for row in relationships_df.itertuples():
    connected_pairs.update({(row.source, row.target), (row.target, row.source)})

added_entities, added_edges, rejected = [], [], []
for document in documents:
    if document["doc_type"] == "faq":
        continue                                           # the 7 long documents contain the relationships
    prompt = EXTRACTION_PROMPT.format(known_names=", ".join(sorted(entity_type_of)), text=document["text"])
    extraction = extractor_llm.invoke(prompt)

    # 1) Entities: known ones are skipped, new ones must literally appear in the document text
    for entity in extraction.entities:
        if resolve_entity(entity.name) is not None:
            continue
        if entity.name.lower() not in document["text"].lower():
            rejected.append((document["doc_id"], entity.name, "name does not appear in the document"))
            continue
        add_entity(entity.name, entity.type, entity.description, source="llm_extracted")
        name_lookup[entity.name.lower()] = entity.name
        entity_type_of[entity.name] = entity.type
        added_entities.append((document["doc_id"], entity.name, entity.type, entity.description))

    # 2) Relations: both ends must resolve, the types must fit the schema, and the pair must be new
    for relation in extraction.relations:
        source_name, target_name = resolve_entity(relation.source), resolve_entity(relation.target)
        description = f"{relation.source} -[{relation.relation}]-> {relation.target}"
        if source_name is None or target_name is None or source_name == target_name:
            rejected.append((document["doc_id"], description, "unknown entity or self-loop"))
            continue
        allowed_sources, allowed_targets = EDGE_SCHEMA[relation.relation]
        if entity_type_of[source_name] not in allowed_sources or entity_type_of[target_name] not in allowed_targets:
            rejected.append((document["doc_id"], description, "entity types do not fit this relation"))
            continue
        if (source_name, target_name) in connected_pairs:
            continue                                       # already known -> keep the curated relationship
        add_relationship(source_name, relation.relation, target_name, source="llm_extracted")
        connected_pairs.update({(source_name, target_name), (target_name, source_name)})
        added_edges.append((document["doc_id"], source_name, relation.relation, target_name))

print(f"The LLM added {len(added_entities)} new entities and {len(added_edges)} new relationships "
      f"({len(rejected)} items were rejected by the validation rules).")
display(pd.DataFrame(added_entities, columns=["found in", "new entity", "type", "description"]))
display(pd.DataFrame(added_edges, columns=["found in", "source", "relation", "target"]))
display(pd.DataFrame(rejected, columns=["found in", "item", "rejected because"]))

3.3 Validate the graph with typical queries¶

Four typical questions, each answered with one Cypher query. The assert statements are small automatic tests: if the graph were wrong, the cell would stop with an error. (We check that the expected answers are included, because the LLM extraction may have added further true facts.)

# Question Pattern
1 Who owns the Payment Gateway? 1 hop: (Person)-[:OWNS]->(System)
2 What does the Checkout Service depend on, directly or indirectly? 1–3 hops DEPENDS_ON
3 What breaks if the Message Queue goes down? 1–3 hops in the reverse direction (impact analysis)
4 Who owns the systems affected by incident INC-2024-021? incident → system ← owner

💡 You can also see the graph: open the Neo4j Browser (http://localhost:7474), select the database capstone and run MATCH (n)-[r]->(m) RETURN n, r, m.

In [22]:
# 1) Simple lookup (1 hop)
owners = [row["owner"] for row in run_cypher(
    "MATCH (p:Person)-[:OWNS]->(:Entity {name: $system}) RETURN p.name AS owner", system="Payment Gateway")]
print("1) Owner of the Payment Gateway:", owners)
assert "Ravi Kumar" in owners

# 2) Multi-hop: all dependencies of the Checkout Service (min(length(path)) = shortest number of hops)
dependencies = run_cypher("""
    MATCH path = (:Entity {name: $system})-[:DEPENDS_ON*1..3]->(dependency:Entity)
    RETURN dependency.name AS dependency, min(length(path)) AS hops
    ORDER BY hops, dependency""", system="Checkout Service")
print("\n2) Checkout Service depends on:\n" + pd.DataFrame(dependencies).to_string(index=False))
assert {"Payment Gateway", "Redis Cache", "Order Database", "Message Queue"} <= {r["dependency"] for r in dependencies}

# 3) Reverse multi-hop = impact analysis: who depends (directly or indirectly) on the Message Queue?
impacted = run_cypher("""
    MATCH path = (affected:Entity)-[:DEPENDS_ON*1..3]->(:Entity {name: $component})
    RETURN affected.name AS affected_system, min(length(path)) AS hops
    ORDER BY hops, affected_system""", component="Message Queue")
print("\n3) Affected if the Message Queue goes down:\n" + pd.DataFrame(impacted).to_string(index=False))
assert {"Notification Service", "Payment Gateway", "Checkout Service"} <= {r["affected_system"] for r in impacted}

# 4) Incident -> affected systems -> their owners
people = run_cypher("""
    MATCH (:Entity {name: $incident})-[:RELATED_TO]->(system:Entity)<-[:OWNS]-(owner:Person)
    RETURN system.name AS affected_system, owner.name AS owner ORDER BY affected_system""", incident="INC-2024-021")
print("\n4) Owners of the systems affected by INC-2024-021:\n" + pd.DataFrame(people).to_string(index=False))
assert {("Redis Cache", "Ben Ortiz"), ("Checkout Service", "Alice Chen"), ("Auth Service", "Tom Becker")} <= \
       {(r["affected_system"], r["owner"]) for r in people}

totals = run_cypher("MATCH (n:Entity) WITH count(n) AS nodes MATCH ()-[r]->() RETURN nodes, count(r) AS relationships")[0]
print(f"\nGraph size: {totals['nodes']} nodes, {totals['relationships']} relationships - all validation queries passed ✅")

4️⃣ Task 4 — Hybrid retrieval: vector + graph, merge, re-rank¶

Each retriever is good at something different:

Retriever Good at Weak at
Vector search (ChromaDB) finding text passages with similar meaning ("rollback rule") chains of facts, exact relationships
Graph traversal (Neo4j) exact relationships and multi-hop chains ("what depends on X?") free text, procedures, numbers in documents

Hybrid retrieval runs both, merges the results, and lets a re-ranker pick the best ones:

question ──► find entities in the question ──► Neo4j: facts around these entities (1–3 hops) ──┐
         └─► ChromaDB: 6 most similar chunks ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─► merge ─► LLM re-ranker ─► top 4 ─► numbered context [1]..[4]

4.1 Graph retrieval: entity linking + traversal¶

  1. Entity linking — find_entities looks for entity names and aliases as whole words in the question. Example: "Is checkout affected when redis is down?" → Checkout Service, Redis Cache.
  2. Traversal — for every entity found, one Cypher query collects: its direct relationships, indirect dependencies over 2–3 hops in both directions (with the chain in between) and the owners of its neighbours (so "who should I contact?" questions work).
  3. The facts are turned into short sentences and returned as one fact chunk per entity, so they can be merged with the text chunks from vector search.
In [23]:
# All graph entities with their aliases (built after Task 3, so it also contains the LLM-extracted entities)
ENTITY_INDEX = run_cypher("MATCH (e:Entity) RETURN e.name AS name, e.type AS type, "
                          "coalesce(e.aliases, []) AS aliases, e.description AS description")


def find_entities(question, limit=5):
    """Return the names of graph entities mentioned in the question (by name or alias, whole words only)."""
    text = question.lower()
    found = []
    for entity in ENTITY_INDEX:
        for term in [entity["name"]] + list(entity["aliases"]):
            # \b = word boundary, so the alias 'mq' does not match inside a word such as 'mqtt'
            if re.search(r"\b" + re.escape(term.lower()) + r"\b", text):
                found.append(entity["name"])
                break                                    # one match per entity is enough
    return found[:limit]


GRAPH_FACTS_QUERY = """
MATCH (e:Entity {name: $name})-[r]-(other:Entity)
RETURN startNode(r).name AS source, type(r) AS relation, endNode(r).name AS target, [] AS via
UNION
MATCH path = (e:Entity {name: $name})-[:DEPENDS_ON*2..3]->(other:Entity)
WHERE NOT (e)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(other)
RETURN e.name AS source, 'INDIRECTLY_DEPENDS_ON' AS relation, other.name AS target,
       [n IN nodes(path)[1..-1] | n.name] AS via
UNION
MATCH path = (other:Entity)-[:DEPENDS_ON*2..3]->(e:Entity {name: $name})
WHERE NOT (other)-[:DEPENDS_ON]->(e)
RETURN other.name AS source, 'INDIRECTLY_DEPENDS_ON' AS relation, e.name AS target,
       [n IN nodes(path)[1..-1] | n.name] AS via
UNION
MATCH (e:Entity {name: $name})--(neighbour:Entity)<-[:OWNS]-(owner:Person)
WHERE owner <> e
RETURN owner.name AS source, 'OWNS' AS relation, neighbour.name AS target, [] AS via
"""
# Part 1: direct relationships | Parts 2+3: indirect dependencies (nodes(path)[1..-1] = the nodes in between)
# Part 4: owners of the neighbours. UNION combines the parts and removes duplicate rows.

RELATION_WORDS = {"OWNS": "owns", "DEPENDS_ON": "depends on", "RELATED_TO": "is related to"}


def fact_sentence(row):
    """Turn one result row into a readable sentence."""
    if row["relation"] == "INDIRECTLY_DEPENDS_ON":
        return f"{row['source']} indirectly depends on {row['target']} (via {' -> '.join(row['via'])})"
    return f"{row['source']} {RELATION_WORDS[row['relation']]} {row['target']}"


def graph_search(question):
    """Return one 'fact chunk' per entity mentioned in the question."""
    hits = []
    for name in find_entities(question):
        entity = next(e for e in ENTITY_INDEX if e["name"] == name)
        facts = [f"{name} is a {entity['type']}: {entity['description']}"]
        for row in run_cypher(GRAPH_FACTS_QUERY, name=name):
            sentence = fact_sentence(row)
            if sentence not in facts:                    # avoid repeating the same fact
                facts.append(sentence)
        hits.append({"id": f"graph::{name}", "text": f"[Knowledge graph: {name}]\n" + "\n".join(f"- {f}" for f in facts),
                     "doc_id": f"graph::{name}", "title": f"Knowledge graph: {name}", "source": "neo4j",
                     "domain": "Graph", "similarity": None, "retriever": "graph"})
    return hits


question = "If the Message Queue goes down, which systems are affected?"
print("Entities found:", find_entities(question))
print(graph_search(question)[0]["text"])

- Ben Ortiz owns Message Queue
- Notification Service depends on Message Queue
- Payment Gateway indirectly depends on Message Queue (via Notification Service)
- Checkout Service indirectly depends on Message Queue (via Payment Gateway -> Notification Service)

4.2 Re-ranking with an LLM¶

The two retrievers produce candidates with incomparable scores: vector hits have a similarity, graph facts have none. A re-ranker reads the question together with every candidate and scores how useful it is for answering it (0 = irrelevant … 10 = directly answers). We use gpt-4o-mini as an LLM re-ranker: one call scores all candidates via structured output. We keep the top 4 with a score of at least 3.

build_context numbers the selected chunks [1], [2], … and adds the source file, so the LLM can cite them and the user can check the answer. Example of a context entry:

[1] (source: refund_policy.pdf | Refund Policy)
[Refund Policy]
4. Approvals
Refunds above 500 USD require approval from the Support Manager. ...
In [24]:
class PassageScore(BaseModel):
    index: int = Field(description="Number of the passage, e.g. 3 for passage [3]")
    score: int = Field(description="Usefulness for answering the question: 0 = irrelevant, 5 = partly useful, "
                                   "10 = directly answers the question")


class RerankResult(BaseModel):
    scores: list[PassageScore]


reranker_llm = ChatOpenAI(model=SIMPLE_MODEL, temperature=0, timeout=90, max_retries=2).with_structured_output(RerankResult)


def rerank(question, candidates, top_n=4, min_score=3):
    """Score every candidate with the LLM, sort best-first and keep the top_n with score >= min_score."""
    if not candidates:
        return []
    numbered = "\n\n".join(f"[{i}] {candidate['text'][:800]}" for i, candidate in enumerate(candidates))
    result = reranker_llm.invoke(
        "Score how useful each passage is for answering the question. Give a score to EVERY passage.\n\n"
        f"Question: {question}\n\nPassages:\n{numbered}")
    scores = {item.index: item.score for item in result.scores}
    scored = []
    for i, candidate in enumerate(candidates):
        copy = dict(candidate)                         # copy, so the original candidate is not modified
        copy["rerank_score"] = scores.get(i, 0)        # a passage the LLM forgot gets 0
        scored.append(copy)
    scored.sort(key=lambda c: c["rerank_score"], reverse=True)       # best first
    return [c for c in scored if c["rerank_score"] >= min_score][:top_n]


def hybrid_retrieve(question, k_vector=6, top_n=4):
    """Vector search + graph traversal -> merge (no duplicates) -> LLM re-ranking."""
    candidates, seen_ids = [], set()
    for hit in graph_search(question) + vector_search(question, k=k_vector):
        if hit["id"] not in seen_ids:
            seen_ids.add(hit["id"])
            candidates.append(hit)
    return rerank(question, candidates, top_n=top_n)


def build_context(chunks):
    """Number the chunks [1], [2], ... with their source, so the answer can cite them."""
    return "\n\n".join(f"[{i}] (source: {chunk['source']} | {chunk['title']})\n{chunk['text']}"
                       for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks, start=1))


rag_llm = ChatOpenAI(model=SIMPLE_MODEL, temperature=0, timeout=90, max_retries=2)


def answer_with_context(question, chunks):
    """A minimal RAG answer: the LLM may only use the numbered context and must cite it."""
    prompt = ("Answer the question using ONLY the numbered context below and cite the sources like [1]. "
              "If the context does not contain the answer, say that you don't know.\n\n"
              f"Context:\n{build_context(chunks)}\n\nQuestion: {question}")
    return rag_llm.invoke(prompt).content


# Look inside: all merged candidates and their scores for a question that needs BOTH retrievers
question = "Who owns the Checkout Service and when must a checkout deployment be rolled back?"
candidates = graph_search(question) + vector_search(question, k=6)
all_scored = rerank(question, candidates, top_n=len(candidates), min_score=0)   # keep all, only to show the scores
pd.DataFrame([{"candidate": c["id"], "retriever": c["retriever"], "vector_similarity": c["similarity"],
               "rerank_score": c["rerank_score"], "selected": i < 4 and c["rerank_score"] >= 3}
              for i, c in enumerate(all_scored)])

4.3 Vector-only vs. hybrid — why the graph matters¶

Now the multi-hop question from the beginning. No document mentions what depends on the Message Queue, so vector search alone cannot answer it, while the hybrid retriever brings the graph facts (with the dependency chains). The second example shows the final context with citations for a question that needs a document and the graph.

In [25]:
question = "If the Message Queue goes down, which systems are affected?"

5️⃣ Task 5 — Agent with tools (LangGraph)¶

Retrieval answers questions about documents. Many questions need actions instead: running SQL, calculating, searching the internet or looking up a support ticket. A tool is a normal Python function plus a description. The LLM reads the descriptions and decides which tool to call with which arguments (tool calling). The agent then runs in a loop until the LLM is satisfied:

question ─► LLM ──"call query_database(sql=...)"──► tool runs ──result──► LLM ──"call run_python(...)"──► ... ─► final answer
Tool (spec name) Our function Example question
Query tool query_database — read-only SQL on PostgreSQL "How many gold tier users do we have?"
Python execution run_python — runs code in a separate Python process "1000 USD at 7 % for 5 years?"
Web search web_search — Tavily search API "What is risk LLM01 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs?"
MCP integration get_ticket, search_tickets, create_ticket from our MCP server "What is the status of ticket TCK-1004?"

5.1 A read-only database user for the SQL tool (least privilege)¶

The LLM writes the SQL for query_database itself, so we must assume it can write bad SQL — by mistake, or because a user tricked it ("...and then delete all users"). The most reliable protection is not a clever check in Python but the database's own permission system: the tool logs in as a separate user kb_reader that may only read. This is the security principle of least privilege — give every component only the rights it really needs.

SQL command (run once by the admin user postgres) Meaning
CREATE ROLE kb_reader LOGIN PASSWORD '...' a new database user (ALTER ROLE if it already exists, so re-running is safe)
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE capstone_kb may connect to our database ...
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public ... may see the tables in the default schema public ...
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public ... may read them — but not insert, update, delete or drop
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES ... GRANT SELECT ON TABLES tables created later (e.g. re-running Task 1) are readable too
REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC ordinary users cannot create new tables in our database

The password comes from .env (POSTGRES_READONLY_PASSWORD) and is inserted with pgsql.Literal(...), which quotes it safely.

In [26]:
READER_USER = os.environ["POSTGRES_READONLY_USER"]           # kb_reader
READER_PASSWORD = os.environ["POSTGRES_READONLY_PASSWORD"]

# Connect as the ADMIN user to OUR database; autocommit=True -> every statement is saved immediately
with psycopg.connect(**PG_SETTINGS, dbname=POSTGRES_DB, autocommit=True) as admin_connection:
    role_exists = admin_connection.execute(
        "SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = %s", (READER_USER,)).fetchone() is not None
    if role_exists:
        role_statement = pgsql.SQL("ALTER ROLE {} LOGIN PASSWORD {}")     # keeps the password in sync with .env
    else:
        role_statement = pgsql.SQL("CREATE ROLE {} LOGIN PASSWORD {}")
    admin_connection.execute(role_statement.format(pgsql.Identifier(READER_USER), pgsql.Literal(READER_PASSWORD)))

    for statement in [
        "GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE {database} TO {user}",
        "GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO {user}",
        "GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO {user}",
        "ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO {user}",
        "REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC",
    ]:
        admin_connection.execute(pgsql.SQL(statement).format(
            database=pgsql.Identifier(POSTGRES_DB), user=pgsql.Identifier(READER_USER)))

    # Show what kb_reader is allowed to do (has_table_privilege is a built-in PostgreSQL function)
    privileges = admin_connection.execute(
        "SELECT table_name, has_table_privilege(%s, table_name, 'SELECT') AS can_select, "
        "has_table_privilege(%s, table_name, 'INSERT') AS can_insert, "
        "has_table_privilege(%s, table_name, 'DELETE') AS can_delete "
        "FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'public' ORDER BY table_name",
        (READER_USER, READER_USER, READER_USER)).fetchall()

print(f"Role {READER_USER!r} {'updated' if role_exists else 'created'}. Its permissions:")
pd.DataFrame(privileges, columns=["table", "can_select", "can_insert", "can_delete"])

5.2 Query, Python and web-search tools (each with safety layers)¶

  • query_database: (1) only SELECT/WITH statements, (2) only one statement (no ; DROP TABLE ...), (3) it connects as the read-only user kb_reader (step 5.1), and (4) the connection is opened in read-only mode with a 10-second time limit (default_transaction_read_only=on, statement_timeout=10000). So PostgreSQL itself refuses every write and every endless query — even if (1) and (2) were tricked. Results are limited to 50 rows.
  • run_python: (1) a deny-list blocks dangerous code (import os, open(, eval( ...), (2) the code runs in a separate process (python -I -S: isolated mode, standard library only) in an empty temporary folder, (3) with a 60-second timeout. ⚠️ This is a simple teaching sandbox, not a perfect security boundary — production systems use containers.
  • web_search: calls the Tavily search API and returns the top 3 results (title, URL, snippet).

The @tool decorator turns a function into a LangChain tool; its docstring becomes the description the LLM reads.

The test calls at the end show each safety layer at work. The interesting one is WITH removed AS (DELETE FROM users RETURNING *) SELECT ... — it starts with WITH and is one statement, so it passes checks (1) and (2). PostgreSQL still refuses it because the connection is read-only (the message says "cannot execute SELECT in a read-only transaction" — the outer statement is a SELECT that hides a DELETE). pg_read_file(...) (reads files on the database server) is refused, too: only an admin may call it, and kb_reader is not an admin.

In [27]:
from langchain_core.tools import tool

# Connection settings of the READ-ONLY user + extra session settings (-c name=value):
# every transaction is read-only, a query may run at most 10 000 ms, and times are shown in UTC
READER_SETTINGS = {**PG_SETTINGS, "user": READER_USER, "password": READER_PASSWORD, "dbname": POSTGRES_DB}
READER_OPTIONS = "-c default_transaction_read_only=on -c statement_timeout=10000 -c TimeZone=UTC"


def run_reader_query(statement, max_rows=50):
    """Run one SQL statement as the read-only user and return (at most max_rows) rows as a DataFrame."""
    with psycopg.connect(**READER_SETTINGS, options=READER_OPTIONS, connect_timeout=10) as connection:
        cursor = connection.execute(statement)        # no parameters -> a '%' in LIKE '%text%' is just a character
        column_names = [column.name for column in cursor.description]
        return pd.DataFrame(cursor.fetchmany(max_rows), columns=column_names)


@tool
def query_database(sql: str) -> str:
    """Run ONE read-only SQL SELECT query on the company PostgreSQL database and return the rows as a table.
    Use it for numbers and facts about products, users, transactions, service logs and document metadata."""
    statement = sql.strip().rstrip(";").strip()
    if not re.match(r"^(select|with)\b", statement, re.IGNORECASE):
        return "Error: only SELECT queries are allowed."
    if ";" in statement:
        return "Error: only one SQL statement is allowed."
    try:
        result = run_reader_query(statement)
    except psycopg.Error as error:              # e.g. a wrong column name -> tell the LLM, so it can fix the query
        return f"SQL error: {str(error).strip()}"
    if result.empty:
        return "The query returned no rows."
    return result.to_markdown(index=False)      # formatted as a Markdown table (easy for the LLM to read)


BLOCKED_MODULES = "os|sys|subprocess|shutil|socket|requests|httpx|urllib|pathlib|ctypes|importlib|pickle|multiprocessing|threading|signal"
BLOCKED_PYTHON_PATTERNS = [
    r"\bimport\s+[\w ,]*\b(" + BLOCKED_MODULES + r")\b",     # import os / import math, os
    r"\bfrom\s+(" + BLOCKED_MODULES + r")\b",                # from os import path
    r"__import__", r"\bopen\s*\(", r"\beval\s*\(", r"\bexec\s*\(", r"\bcompile\s*\(",
    r"\bglobals\s*\(", r"\bgetattr\s*\(", r"\bbreakpoint\s*\(", r"\binput\s*\(",
]


@tool
def run_python(code: str) -> str:
    """Execute Python code for calculations and return everything it prints. Always print() the result.
    Only the Python standard library is available (math, statistics, datetime, json ...); no files, network or system access."""
    for pattern in BLOCKED_PYTHON_PATTERNS:
        if re.search(pattern, code):
            return f"Error: this code is not allowed (blocked pattern: {pattern})"
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as work_dir:          # an empty folder that is deleted afterwards
        try:
            completed = subprocess.run(
                [sys.executable, "-I", "-S", "-c", code],      # -I = isolated mode, -S = no extra packages
                capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60, cwd=work_dir)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            return "Error: the code ran longer than 60 seconds and was stopped."
    output = (completed.stdout + completed.stderr).strip()
    if not output:
        return "The code ran but printed nothing. Use print(...) to show the result."
    return output[:2000]                                     # keep tool results short for the LLM


@tool
def web_search(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the public internet for external or current information that is NOT in the company knowledge base,
    e.g. public standards, regulations, technologies or news."""
    response = httpx.post(
        "https://api.tavily.com/search",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['TAVILY_API_KEY']}"},
        json={"query": query, "max_results": 3},
        timeout=30,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()                              # turn HTTP errors (401, 500 ...) into exceptions
    results = response.json().get("results", [])
    if not results:
        return "No web results found."
    return "\n\n".join(f"[web {i}] {r['title']} ({r['url']})\n{r['content'][:600]}"
                       for i, r in enumerate(results, start=1))
